planting.note: Source only nursery-propagated, lab-cultured plants from a reputable native orchid specialist and plant in fall in humus-rich, well-drained but consistently moist woodland soil in dappled shade; this species depends on a specific mycorrhizal fungal partner in the root zone and will not persist without it, so never disturb an established planting once sited.

directions: Mountain lady's slipper is native to coniferous and mixed forests of the Pacific Northwest and northern Rockies, from British Columbia south through the Cascades and Sierra Nevada into Montana and Wyoming, where it flowers from late spring into midsummer depending on elevation. Each stem carries one to three flowers with twisted, maroon-brown sepals and petals surrounding a white, purple-veined pouch, growing in humus-rich but well-drained duff on shaded slopes. This is a genuinely difficult species to keep alive in a garden setting because it relies on a narrow set of soil fungi found in undisturbed forest floors, so success depends heavily on replicating cool, dappled-shade, well-aerated conditions and starting only with nursery-propagated stock, never wild-dug plants. Even under good conditions, expect slow establishment and be prepared for occasional non-blooming years.

planting.note: Use only nursery-propagated plants and site in cool, consistently moist, calcium-rich soil near a woodland stream or seep in partial shade; like all Cypripedium it depends on a specific soil mycorrhizal fungus to survive and cannot be reliably grown from wild-collected divisions.

directions: Sparrow's-egg lady's slipper is a small, boreal species native to Alaska and across northern Canada, reaching the contiguous United States only in scattered cold, high-elevation sites in the northern Rockies, where it grows along gravelly streambanks and moist, calcareous woods in spruce-fir forest. It blooms in early summer with a compact white pouch delicately speckled with fine purple or reddish spots, giving rise to its evocative common name. It is among the least commercially available native lady's slippers, its cold-hardiness and calcium-rich, constantly moist soil requirements making it a poor fit for most home gardens outside cold, northern climates. Only attempt this species with nursery-propagated stock and be prepared for a very narrow band of success even then.

planting.note: Plant only nursery-propagated stock in fall into constantly saturated, humus-rich soil that mimics a natural seep, in partial shade; this species depends on specific mycorrhizal fungi and rarely tolerates drying out even briefly, so a boggy, spring-fed or irrigated site is essential.

directions: California lady's slipper is a narrow endemic of serpentine seeps and streamside fens in far northern California and southwestern Oregon, where clumps send up tall stems bearing several small, greenish-white flowers with a contrasting white pouch from April into June. Unlike most of its relatives it naturally grows with its roots in constantly running or saturated water, so a home planting needs a permanently wet seep, spring line, or irrigated bog bed rather than typical woodland soil. It still requires its native mycorrhizal fungi to persist long-term and should only be sourced as nursery-propagated material, since wild populations are localized and sensitive to disturbance. Give it full sun to light shade with cool root conditions and expect a multi-year wait before it forms a floriferous clump.

planting.note: Plant nursery-propagated tubers in spring into consistently moist to wet, humus-rich soil in full sun to partial shade; never dig from the wild, and expect the planting to depend on native soil mycorrhizal fungi for long-term persistence.

directions: Small purple fringed orchid is native to wet meadows, fens, streambanks, and open woodland edges across northeastern and north-central North America, from the Canadian Maritimes and Great Lakes south through the Appalachians. In midsummer it produces a dense spike of fragrant, lavender-purple flowers with a deeply fringed lip that is a favorite of clearwing moths and butterflies. It needs steadily moist to wet, humus-rich soil and resents any drying out, and like most native orchids will not survive long without its specific soil fungi already present. Buy only nursery-propagated plants and place them in a consistently damp meadow or bog-garden setting rather than ordinary garden beds.

planting.note: Plant nursery-propagated tubers in spring into rich, consistently moist to wet soil in partial shade to full sun; this species depends on its associated soil mycorrhizae and should never be sourced from wild populations.

directions: Large purple fringed orchid grows in wet meadows, seepage slopes, and open swampy woods across the northeastern United States and adjacent Canada, extending south at higher elevations through the Appalachians, and flowers from early to midsummer just ahead of the closely related small purple fringed orchid. Its spikes carry larger, more showily fringed lavender-purple flowers with a wider lip and are pollinated mainly by large hawkmoths and butterflies. It demands the same rich, evenly moist to wet soil and cool root run as other native fringed orchids and is equally dependent on its native mycorrhizal partner to persist beyond a season or two. Plant only nursery-propagated stock in a consistently wet meadow or bog-garden bed, and treat any bloom in the first few years as a bonus rather than an expectation.

planting.note: Plant nursery-propagated tubers in spring into moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in full sun to partial shade; source only from specialist native orchid growers, since this species depends on soil mycorrhizal fungi and wild collection is both illegal in many states and ecologically harmful.

directions: Ragged fringed orchid has the widest range of the eastern fringed orchids, found in wet meadows, old fields, roadside ditches, and boggy openings from Maine and Ontario south to Florida and Texas, blooming in mid to late summer. Its pale greenish-white flowers have a lip so finely and irregularly fringed it looks torn, giving the plant its common name, and it is pollinated mainly by night-flying moths. Despite its broader range compared to other native orchids, it is no easier to establish in cultivation, since it still needs consistently moist, acidic soil and its specific mycorrhizal fungi to survive past the first year. Grow it only from nursery-propagated stock in a damp, sunny to lightly shaded meadow setting, and avoid any soil disturbance once it is planted.

planting.note: Plant nursery-propagated tubers in spring into consistently wet, mineral-rich soil at a seep, streambank, or bog-garden edge in partial shade to full sun; it needs its native soil mycorrhizae to thrive and should never be sourced from wild-dug material.

directions: White bog orchid has one of the broadest ranges of any North American Platanthera, spanning Alaska and the Rocky Mountain and Pacific states east through the boreal forest to New England and the Great Lakes, growing in wet meadows, streamside seeps, and montane bogs from low to fairly high elevations. It blooms from early to late summer depending on latitude and elevation, producing a spike of small, intensely fragrant white flowers that give it the nickname scent bottle. It tolerates a somewhat wider range of soil chemistry than many bog orchids but still needs constantly saturated soil and its native fungal associates to persist, so it is not a plant for ordinary garden beds. Establish it only from nursery-propagated stock in a permanently damp seep or bog-garden feature, and expect slow, incremental spread rather than quick results.

planting.note: Plant nursery-propagated tubers in spring into wet, acidic, sandy or peaty soil in full sun; source only from reputable native plant nurseries, since this species depends on mycorrhizal fungi and wild coastal-plain populations are increasingly scarce.

directions: Snowy orchid grows in open, sunny wet pine savannas, seepage bogs, and roadside ditches on the Atlantic and Gulf Coastal Plain from the Carolinas south to Florida and west to Texas, flowering from spring into early summer depending on latitude. It sends up a dense, tapering spike of small, pure white flowers above narrow grass-like foliage, standing out sharply against the surrounding wiregrass and sedges of its savanna habitat. Unlike the shade-tolerant wood orchids, it needs full sun and constantly wet, nutrient-poor, acidic sandy soil to compete successfully, conditions that are difficult to replicate outside a dedicated bog garden. Plant only nursery-propagated stock, keep it wet with rainwater or distilled water rather than tap water, and pair it with pitcher plants or sundews in a sunny, boggy bed.
